source.title: Sample Variance Decay in Randomly Initialized ReLU Networks

record.file_problem: Full text is present. Some OCR or typesetting artifacts appear, but the relevant results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares data-dependent initialization schemes and measures their effect on training speed, a different method and measure bearing on V4.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports sample-variance ratios and gradient behavior at initialization. Those measures do not directly test the training-error, depth, or batch-normalization-speed outcomes named in the versions, so they are not rows. Training-speed comparisons are reported in Figure 4; exact values are not stated in the text.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares training-loss trajectories under two initialization schemes, testing V4's training-speed component. Figure 4 also includes batch-normalized networks, providing a comparison relevant to V6, although its relative outcomes cannot be recovered from the supplied text.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate for the training experiments: preserving sample mean and variance at initialization yields faster training than preserving total variance alone in all four tested settings. The broader conclusion distinguishes sample variance from total variance and shows that sample-variance preservation can produce exploding gradients at initialization.
record.recipe_differences: Uses data-dependent, per-layer scale and per-feature bias initialization, then compares training loss; it does not test the activation-matched or orthogonal initializations described in V4.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported comparisons span two architectures, two datasets, and SGD or Adam; the text reports a speed gain for scale+bias initialization in each case.

fits_no_version.finding: Kaiming initialization preserves total variance while sample variance decays with depth; batch normalization prevents sample-variance decay. In separate untrained 50-layer MLP experiments, scale+bias initialization and batch normalization produce exponentially growing backward gradients.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Preserving total activation variance need not preserve variation across inputs, and preserving sample variance can coexist with exploding gradients at initialization.

record.problems: Training-speed results are presented as plots without exact values. The text reports standard deviations over three runs but gives no statistical test. Experiments cover two architectures and datasets.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Initialization sample-variance and gradient measurements were excluded because they do not measure the training outcomes named by the claim versions.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training classification error, random or corrupted labels, CIFAR-100, and model-size or regularization effects.
Teacher-student ReLU optimization, spurious local minima, and benefits of extra student neurons.
Training-error degradation with increasing depth and its prevention by identity residual shortcuts or the specified alternative recipes.

Trainable-depth comparisons, activation-function comparisons, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, and 10,000-layer convolutional networks. The speed experiments do not establish that avoiding gradient explosion causes faster training.
Stability thresholds, catapult recovery, sharpness dynamics during training, and divergence.

Accuracy trajectories, higher-learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons. Batch-normalization training-loss comparisons are present, but their outcomes are unreadable in the supplied figure extraction.

missing.what: Batch-normalized versus unnormalized training-loss trajectories for both architectures and both optimizers are included in Figure 4 but omitted from the rows. The supplied extraction contains no readable curves or explicit statement of their relative performance, so a V6 verdict cannot be assigned.

record.verdict_notes: No exact loss differences or statistical significance tests are supplied. The initialization-statistic and gradient experiments were explicitly declared omitted by the reader; they do not independently establish training-speed or trainable-depth outcomes.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error, CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, and the stated model-size and training-duration conditions.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious local minima, and extra student neurons.
Training error as a function of depth, identity shortcuts preventing degradation, and the specified plain-network recipes.

Activation-matched initializations, comparisons of orthogonal and Gaussian weights, and training at greater depth. The study tests data-dependent sample-statistic initializations and their training-speed effects.
Learning rates above a stability limit, curvature dynamics, and divergence.

Whether batch normalization speeds training or tolerates higher learning rates compared with the same networks without it; the paper includes batch normalization in its comparison but states a speed result only for scale+bias versus scale initialization.
